idiom_name: interface Renderer + abstract class Shape (JDBC-style split)
implementation_notes: The implementor is an interface, the abstraction an abstract class (or a plain class) holding it, and refined abstractions extend the abstraction. The JDK's own instance of the pattern is JDBC, where java.sql is the abstraction and each vendor driver implements java.sql.Driver, discovered through META-INF/services/java.sql.Driver by ServiceLoader since Java 6; java.util.logging routes handlers the same way. What replaces the classic structure in application code is constructor injection plus a DI framework or a service loader to choose the implementor, leaving the abstraction with one forwarded reference. Keep the classic abstract-class hierarchy when refined abstractions share forwarding logic, and remember that every forwarded call is virtual: the JIT inlines monomorphic sites, so the split is free in ordinary code but visible in hot loops with many implementors.
pitfalls: Constructing the concrete implementor inside the abstraction (new CairoRenderer() in the constructor) hard-wires the mechanism again; inject it or take it from a factory or service loader.
ServiceLoader discovery fails silently when a provider JAR lacks META-INF/services/java.sql.Driver, leaving the wrong implementor or none: assert the loaded providers at startup.
Forwarded calls are virtual; after JIT warm-up a monomorphic call site is inlined, but a megamorphic implementor call in a hot loop is measurably slower - measure before splitting a hot primitive.

variants.name: Sealed implementor interface with an exhaustive pattern switch
variants.implementation_notes: Model the implementors as permitted final records of a sealed interface (sealed is final since Java 17) and dispatch with a pattern switch, which became a permanent feature in Java 21; the compiler computes type coverage over the sealed hierarchy, so no default branch is needed and adding an implementor is a compile error at every dispatch site. This trades openness for exhaustiveness and removes the vtable indirection of the classic form, which is the right trade when you own every implementor.
pitfalls: A sealed hierarchy plus exhaustive switches means every new implementor breaks compilation of every dispatch site - excellent safety, but extension by third parties becomes impossible.

Adding a default branch (or a null case) silences the exhaustiveness check that justified the sealed design; a switch that was exhaustive at compile time but not at run time throws MatchException after a hierarchy change.
Records in the sealed set are value types, so implementor state that must be shared or mutated has to live outside the record or the exhaustiveness benefit is paid for nothing.
